Unilateral

/yoo-nuh-LAT-er-ul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Unilateral means done by one side alone, without the agreement or consent of the others involved — one-sided action where cooperation was expected.

Employees were stunned by the CEO's unilateral decision to cancel the remote-work policy overnight.

Worked Example

Without checking with his roommates, Theo made the unilateral choice to repaint their shared kitchen bright orange while they were away for the weekend.

The kitchen belongs to everyone, so everyone expected a say — but Theo acted entirely on his own. Unilateral flags a one-sided action taken where agreement was expected.

How Unilateral Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

one-sided

one-sided: coming from a single side only

solo

solo: done by one person or party alone

independent

independent: acting without others' input

Antonyms

mutual

mutual: shared and agreed by both sides

joint

joint: done together by two or more parties

How Strong Is It? — independent → unilateral → dictatorial

independent vs. unilateral

independent vs. unilateral: An independent choice is simply made on your own; a unilateral one is made alone when others expected a say.

dictatorial vs. unilateral

dictatorial vs. unilateral: A unilateral decision skips the group once, but a dictatorial leader silences the group every single time.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — uni-

Prefix — uni-: one (from Latin unus)

Root — -later-

Root — -later-: side (from Latin latus, lateris)

Suffix — -al

Suffix — -al: adjective-forming: 'relating to'

Put it together

Put it together: Unilateral literally means 'relating to one side' — an action launched from a single side of the table while the other sides look on without a vote.

Use the root in a new word: bilateral

Use the root in a new word: bilateral: After months of talks, the two countries reached a bilateral agreement that both parliaments celebrated.

Root Check

Word Choice

Formal — political, often critical

Unilateral is this unit's deliberate odd one out: while most Unit 11 words describe sides coming together, unilateral describes one side acting alone, without the consent of the others involved — and it often carries a critical edge ('a unilateral decision' hints that others should have been consulted). Its natural opposites are the unit's own cooperation words: mutual and reciprocal describe exactly what unilateral actions lack, and multilateral describes many parties acting together.
